timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So HTTPS is just HTTP with a lock icon?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: HTTPS is HTTP encrypted with TLS. The lock means your data is encrypted in transit. No lock means plaintext.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What happens if I visit a site without HTTPS?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Every request and response travels in plain text. Anyone on the network — WiFi router, ISP, attacker — can read it all.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: But what about mixed content? I've seen warnings about that.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: If a page loads over HTTPS but includes an HTTP resource, that one resource is vulnerable. Attackers can hijack it.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Even if the main page is secure?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Yes. One HTTP script on an HTTPS page is like locking your front door but leaving a window open.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What about cookies? Aren't those just harmless trackers?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Session cookies are the keys to your account. Without Secure and HttpOnly flags, they can be stolen over HTTP or by XSS.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: HTTP Strict Transport Security tells the browser to never connect via HTTP again. It prevents protocol downgrade attacks.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So there's a lot more to HTTPS than just the certificate?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: The certificate is step one. Headers, cookies, and configuration are what make it actually secure.
